6612: Augustine changed his mind. Early on he said such miracles were not permitted to continue (*On True Religion* 25.47) and that tongues had passed away (*Homilies on 1 John* 6.10), but later he catalogued many healings at Hippo and elsewhere (*City of God* 22.8) and qualified his earlier remark in his *Retractations*.

6622: Cessationists agree no verse states the timing directly, but argue that a cumulative case (foundation, authentication, revelatory character, sufficiency of Scripture, historical observation) is legitimate, just as the closing of the canon is itself inferred rather than stated. 6624: Cessationists reply that Pentecost fulfils Joel in the once-for-all outpouring of the Spirit, and that what continues is the gift of the Spirit himself to all believers (Acts 2:38), not every phenomenon that accompanied his first coming.
6625: Cessationists do not believe God does miracles today.
6626: Cessationists affirm that God heals and works wonders in answer to prayer; they deny that the specific gifts of revelation and sign-working given to individuals continue.
6627: Cessationists believe the Holy Spirit is no longer active.
6628: Cessationists teach the ongoing indwelling, illumination, sanctification and gifting (teaching, service, mercy, leadership) of the Spirit in every believer.
6629: Cessationism rests entirely on reading 1 Cor 13:10 as the canon.
6630: Many leading cessationists reject that reading and rely on the foundation, authentication and sufficiency arguments instead.
6631: Guards the sufficiency and finality of Scripture.
6632: Provides a check on fraud, manipulation and unverified revelatory claims.
6633: Focuses ministry on the word, prayer and ordinary means of grace.
6634: Can foster scepticism toward genuine answers to prayer or a low expectation of God's activity.

6636: Critics argue it reads a theological system into texts that do not state cessation.

6638: Old Princeton (Charles Hodge, B. B. Warfield)
6640: Contemporary: Richard Gaffin, John MacArthur, O. Palmer Robertson, Thomas Schreiner, many Presbyterian and Reformed churches, Grace Community Church and The Master's Seminary
6642:
Continuationism holds that all the gifts of the Spirit listed in the New Testament, including prophecy, tongues, interpretation, healing and miracles, remain available to the church until Christ returns. The 'last days' inaugurated at Pentecost continue throughout the church age, and nothing in Scripture says the gifts would be withdrawn earlier.

Many non-Pentecostal continuationists (e.g. Grudem, Storms) distinguish New Testament congregational prophecy, which is a human report of something God spontaneously brings to mind and must be tested, from the authoritative revelation of the apostles and Scripture, so that continuing gifts do not threaten the closed canon. Pentecostals and charismatics share the conviction of continuing gifts while often adding distinctive teaching on Spirit baptism.
6644: Founding leader of the Vineyard movement
6645: A former musician and church-growth consultant, Wimber taught the 'Signs, Wonders and Church Growth' course at Fuller Theological Seminary (from 1982) and led the 'Third Wave' movement: evangelicals who embraced the gifts without adopting classical Pentecostal theology of a second blessing.
6648: Systematic theologian (Trinity Evangelical Divinity School, Phoenix Seminary)
6649: Grudem's doctoral work at Cambridge argued that New Testament congregational prophecy has a different authority from Old Testament prophecy and apostolic teaching: it is fallible, to be evaluated, and does not add to Scripture. He edited the Four Views volume that popularised the categories used in this debate.
6652: Pastor and theologian, former president of the Evangelical Theological Society
6653: A Reformed theologian who moved from cessationism to continuationism through involvement with the Vineyard; he wrote the 'Third Wave' essay in the Four Views volume and many books arguing for a biblically regulated practice of the gifts.
6655: Former Old Testament professor at Dallas Theological Seminary
6656: Deere left Dallas Seminary after becoming convinced that the gifts continue; his widely read book argues that Christians are cessationists not because of Scripture but because of a lack of experience, and critically engages the cessationist case.
6659: New Testament scholar, Asbury Theological Seminary
6660: Keener's two-volume study collects historical and contemporary miracle claims worldwide, arguing that eyewitness reports of healings are widespread and that the New Testament accounts are therefore credible; he has also written on the Spirit's gifts from a Pentecostal-friendly evangelical perspective.
6661: Claims of continuing gifts appear in the second and third centuries (Irenaeus, Justin, Tertullian), were complicated by the Montanist controversy, and recur in various renewal movements. The modern movement began with Pentecostalism (Topeka, 1901; Azusa Street, Los Angeles, 1906), spread into mainline and Catholic churches through the charismatic renewal (from 1960), and among evangelicals through the 'Third Wave' associated with John Wimber in the 1980s. Reformed and evangelical theologians such as D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones (in sermons published as *Joy Unspeakable*, 1984), Wayne Grudem and Sam Storms argued from Scripture that the gifts had not ceased. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians now number in the hundreds of millions, especially in the Global South.

6663: 2. 'The perfect' of 1 Cor 13:10 is the state brought about by Christ's return, when we will see face to face; until then, prophecy and tongues continue.

6666: 5. Miracles express God's compassion and the presence of the kingdom, not merely the authentication of apostles.
6667: 6. The gifts should be pursued eagerly and exercised in an orderly way under the authority of Scripture.
6668: The gifts cease when the perfect comes and we see face to face, which is Christ’s return; until then they remain.
6669: Pursue love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy: a standing command to the church.
6670: Earnestly desire to prophesy and do not forbid speaking in tongues.

6672: The promise is for you, your children and all who are far off: later generations are included.
6673: Gifts including healing, miracles, prophecy and tongues are given to ordinary members for the common good.
6674: Do not quench the Spirit or despise prophecies, but test everything: prophecy is fallible and must be weighed.

6688: Heb 2:3-4 speaks of the gospel being confirmed in the past by signs given to the first generation of hearers, implying their attesting role was complete.
6689: The rise of excesses, false prophecies, prosperity teaching and abuses in charismatic movements shows the danger of claiming continuing revelatory gifts.
6690: Continuationists sometimes identify modern phenomena too quickly with the New Testament gifts and treat them as normal expectations for every believer, without sufficient discernment or attention to the diversity of the gifts.
6691: Carson and others argue that charismatic theology often rests on doctrines (Spirit baptism as a second blessing, tongues as initial evidence) that are poorly supported by 1 Cor 12–14, even if the gifts themselves continue.
6692: Grudem and Storms reply that the New Testament itself treats congregational prophecy as subject to evaluation (1 Cor 14:29; 1 Thess 5:20-21), distinguishes it from apostolic authority (1 Cor 14:37-38), and records a prophecy accurate in substance but inexact in detail (Acts 21:11). Deut 18 concerns those claiming to speak with divine authority in the Lord's name.
6693: Continuationists note that Eph 2:20 may refer to apostles who are also prophets (one group) or to the specific prophets of the apostolic circle, and that 1 Cor 12–14 describes a wider congregational gift of prophecy that is not foundational.

6695: Continuationists say the verse describes how the readers received the message, not that signs must stop; Hebrews is silent about whether they continued.
6696: Continuationists such as Storms and Grudem openly criticise abuses and the prosperity gospel, but argue that misuse calls for biblical regulation (1 Cor 14), not prohibition; Paul corrected Corinthian disorder without forbidding the gifts.
6697: Thoughtful continuationists agree that not all speak in tongues (1 Cor 12:30), that experiences must be tested, and that the gifts should be desired rather than demanded. They accept caution as a virtue but regard the default stance of the New Testament as eager pursuit.
6698: Third Wave continuationists (Wimber, Grudem, Storms) largely agree and reject subsequence and initial-evidence teaching; they argue for continuing gifts on exegetical grounds independent of classical Pentecostal theology.
6699: Continuationists believe modern prophecies are equal to Scripture.
6700: Most evangelical continuationists explicitly deny this, teaching that Scripture is closed and uniquely authoritative and that prophecy must be tested by it.
6701: Continuationism means endorsing everything done in the name of the Spirit.
6702: Continuationist scholars frequently critique fraud, manipulation and prosperity teaching, and call for the orderly exercise of gifts.
6703: Continuationists are all Pentecostals who teach a second blessing.
6704: Many continuationists (Reformed charismatics, Third Wave) reject subsequence and initial-evidence doctrines.
6705: Encourages expectant prayer, including for healing.
6706: Has fuelled extraordinary church growth in the Global South.
6707: Revived attention to the person and work of the Holy Spirit in worship and mission.
6708: Can open the door to unaccountable revelatory claims and manipulation.
6709: Associated in some streams with prosperity teaching and celebrity leaders.
6710: Can create two tiers of Christians or disappointment when healings do not occur.

6712: Pentecostal denominations (Assemblies of God, Church of God in Christ, Foursquare)
6715: Reformed charismatics (e.g. Sovereign Grace Churches, Newfrontiers)
6716: Contemporary: Wayne Grudem, Sam Storms, Craig Keener, Gordon Fee, John Piper (who describes himself as open to the gifts), D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones (earlier)
6718:
The 'open but cautious' position holds that Scripture does not teach that the miraculous gifts have ceased, so Christians should be open to God giving them today; but it is cautious about identifying contemporary phenomena with the New Testament gifts, about the theology often attached to them, and about practices that can lead to error or division.

The label comes from Robert L. Saucy's contribution to *Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views* (ed. Wayne Grudem, 1996). D. A. Carson's exegetical study *Showing the Spirit* (1987), which rejects the main cessationist arguments while criticising charismatic theology, is often grouped with it.
6720: Systematic theologian, Talbot School of Theology
6721: A progressive dispensational theologian who wrote the 'open but cautious' essay in the Four Views volume. He argued that Scripture does not prove cessation, but that the miraculous gifts were especially concentrated in the apostolic era and that the church should be careful in claiming them now.
6724: New Testament scholar, Trinity Evangelical Divinity School
6725: Carson's exposition of 1 Corinthians 12–14 concludes that the cessationist exegesis of 1 Cor 13:8-10 fails and that the gifts may continue, while challenging charismatic doctrines of a second blessing and tongues as initial evidence and urging mutual charity between the camps.
6728: Packer gave a sympathetic but critical evaluation of the charismatic renewal, commending its spiritual vitality while questioning its theology and some practices, and urging openness alongside careful discernment.
6730: Anglican rector of All Souls, Langham Place, and evangelical leader
6731: Stott's short study argued against a post-conversion baptism in the Spirit as a separate experience, while acknowledging the sovereign freedom of the Spirit in distributing gifts; he became a moderating voice in British evangelical debates over renewal.
6732: As the charismatic renewal spread into evangelical churches in the 1960s–1980s, many leaders found neither strict cessationism nor full charismatic practice persuasive. British evangelicals (Stott, Packer) navigated tensions in the Church of England, and in America the Third Wave prompted fresh exegetical work. The Four Views volume (1996) presented four positions: cessationist (Gaffin), open but cautious (Saucy), Third Wave (Storms) and Pentecostal/charismatic (Douglas Oss), with mutual responses. Many evangelical churches today effectively operate in this space.

6736: 4. Charismatic doctrines such as subsequence and initial evidence are not well supported by Scripture.
6737: 5. Believers should be open to God working miraculously, especially in pioneering mission, while prioritising Scripture, love and the ordinary means of grace.
6738: 6. The question should not divide churches; unity and charity should govern disagreements.

6741: Test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out: a call to caution.

6744: Gifts without love are nothing: love is the controlling priority.
6745: Miracles had a special attesting role with the first witnesses, supporting the expectation that they were concentrated then.

6751: Openness avoids limiting God's sovereignty, and caution protects the sufficiency of Scripture and the health of the church.
